title: The Grandfather's Library to the Mount of Those Who Rest: Buber, the Hasidic Tales, and the Word Between
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Vienna, Franz-Josefs-Kai 45: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the house address is fixed by the plaque of 12 June 1990 and corrects an earlier Josefstadt attribution
stops.campa: On the Franz-Josefs-Kai, in the first district of Vienna, a son is born to Carl Buber and Elise Wurgast on the eighth of February 1878. The family is assimilated and observant at once, prosperous, and about to come apart. A plaque set into the wall of this house in 1990 will name the boy a philosopher and give both his dates, the Vienna one and the Jerusalem one, as though the whole life were a single sentence. He is three or four years old when his mother leaves and the sentence begins its long detour east.
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque at Franz-Josefs-Kai 45, Innere Stadt, unveiled 12 June 1990 by the Kulturverein Innere Stadt

stops.name: Lemberg, the house of Solomon Buber
stops.date_confidence: year inferred; Wikipedia gives his age at the separation as three, the Stanford Encyclopedia as four, and the conflict is not resolved. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is sent east to Lemberg, to his father's parents, and grows up in the house of Solomon Buber, editor of midrash, landowner, one of the last great scholars of the Galician Haskalah. The library is the childhood. Hebrew comes to him there, Yiddish in the street, Polish and German and Greek and Latin at the Kaiser-Franz-Joseph-Gymnasium, so that by fourteen he crosses five languages without noticing the borders. His grandmother Adele runs the house and the reading. His mother does not come back.
stops.quote: Time was not a sentence hanging over me; it was mine, for it was 'ours.'
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, Autobiographical Fragments, in Schilpp and Friedman eds., The Philosophy of Martin Buber (1972), pp. 11-13, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
suggested_refs: Solomon Buber's editions of the midrashim, printed at Vilna and Lemberg
The Kaiser-Franz-Joseph-Gymnasium of Lemberg, building unlocated in consulted sources
sources: Maurice Friedman, Martin Buber's Life and Work

stops.name: Lemberg, the Prolegomena and Zarathustra
stops.date_confidence: the Stanford Encyclopedia states 'Age 15: read Kant's Prolegomena', which puts it in 1893 and corrects an earlier 1892; the Nietzsche reading is dated to about age 17, so 1895. Both merged here, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At fifteen he reads Kant's Prolegomena and the ground gives way: space and time turn into the forms of his own looking rather than the walls of the world, and the infinite regress he has been lying awake inside stops. At seventeen he reads Thus Spoke Zarathustra and is seized the other way, into time as flow and eternal return. He will call the first a rescue and the second a seduction he had to work himself free of. Both books arrive in a house full of midrash, and neither is read there for comfort.
suggested_refs: Kant, Prolegomena zu einer jeden kunftigen Metaphysik, read at fifteen
Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra, read at seventeen

stops.name: Vienna, matriculation at the university
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted. Coordinate is the canonical Vienna pin shared with the Freud, Steiner, Keyserling and Itten journeys, not the university building
stops.campa: He comes back to the city he was born in and enrolls in philosophy, art history, German studies and philology. Vienna in 1896 is a small room with many doors. Sigmund Freud is four years from the dream book and a walk away in the ninth district; Rudolf Steiner is at work on the Goethe edition. By his own account Buber learns more about the word passing between two people from the theatre than from any lecture hall. He is eighteen, fluent in the languages of two empires, and at home in neither.
suggested_refs: The University of Vienna matriculation registers, winter semester 1896

stops.name: Leipzig, the Zionist association
stops.date_confidence: the year 1898 for joining the movement is attested; the place is corrected from Vienna to Leipzig, where the Stanford Encyclopedia puts him for 1897-98. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He moves to Leipzig for a year and joins the Zionist movement there, through the student association rather than through any congress hall. What draws him is Nathan Birnbaum's cultural Zionism, the argument that a people has to be made before a state can hold it. Theodor Herzl is building the other kind, the diplomatic kind, and Buber will work for him and quarrel with him inside three years. He does not meet Herzl face to face until February 1900, by which time the disagreement is already formed.
suggested_refs: The Leipzig Zionist student association, 1897-1898

stops.name: Berlin, the lectures of Dilthey and Simmel
stops.date_confidence: the Stanford Encyclopedia gives Berlin 1898-99; the October start is the ordinary winter semester and is inferred. Coordinate is the canonical Berlin pin
stops.campa: Berlin for the next year, and two teachers who mark him for good. Wilhelm Dilthey reads a life from inside its own understanding. Georg Simmel reads society as the forms taken by whatever passes between people. Felix Adler had studied the critical science of Judaism in this same city a quarter of a century before carrying Ethical Culture to New York. From Simmel, Buber takes the word Zwischen, the between, and will spend forty years making it hold more weight than a preposition should.
suggested_refs: Georg Simmel's Berlin lectures on the forms of sociation, late 1890s

stops.name: Zurich, Paula Winkler
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: A term at Zurich, and in it Paula Winkler: Bavarian, Catholic by birth, a writer who will publish her own novels and stories under the name Georg Munk. She leaves the Church in 1901 and converts to Judaism before the marriage. Two children come first, Rafael in 1900 and Eva in 1901, so the household precedes the wedding by years and the conversion by more. For fifty-nine years she reads everything he writes before anyone else is allowed to see it, and he says so in print, repeatedly.
suggested_refs: The novels and stories of Georg Munk, the pen name of Paula Buber

stops.name: Basel, the Stadtcasino and the Democratic Faction
stops.date_confidence: Third Congress August 1899, Fifth Congress December 1901, both in this hall; his attendance is documented from the Third onward and the day is not specified
stops.campa: In the concert hall of the Stadtcasino, where Herzl convened the first congress two years earlier, Buber sits with the Democratic Faction: the young men who want schools, a press and a Hebrew culture before they want a charter from any Sultan. He speaks on propaganda and on education, which for this faction are the same subject seen from two ends. He is back in the same hall for the Fifth Congress. The faction loses its argument with Herzl in the room and wins it across the century that follows.
suggested_refs: The Stadtcasino concert hall at Basel, seat of the early Zionist Congresses

stops.name: Vienna, the editorship of Die Welt
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives 'Redakteur der Die Welt ab September 1901', correcting an earlier 1902; the editorial office address is unconfirmed and the coordinate is Vienna city centre
stops.campa: Herzl hands the twenty-three-year-old the editorship of Die Welt, the central organ of the movement, in September. Buber fills it with art, literature and the Jewish renaissance he has in mind. Herzl wants a political weekly and says so. The editorship lasts months rather than years, and the break is structural before it is personal: one man is making a state and the other is making a people, and a single paper cannot carry both programmes on the same page without one of them looking like decoration.
suggested_refs: The 1901-1902 volumes of Die Welt under Buber's editorship

stops.name: Vienna, the doctorate on Cusa and Boehme
stops.date_confidence: some sources date the dissertation 1903 and others 1904; not resolved. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He withdraws from the movement's committees and finishes a dissertation on the problem of individuation in Nicholas of Cusa and Jakob Boehme, two thinkers for whom God and the world are folded into one another. The degree is taken at Vienna. Behind him lie six years of organisational work; ahead of him lie five years of near silence in which he reads Hasidic texts and publishes almost nothing. He is twenty-six and has just made his subject out of German mysticism rather than Jewish politics.
suggested_refs: Buber's Vienna dissertation, Zur Geschichte des Individuationsproblems: Nicolaus von Cues und Jakob Boehme

stops.name: Berlin, Rutten and Loening and the Judischer Verlag
stops.date_confidence: the Gesellschaft series runs from 1906 to 1912; the Judischer Verlag was founded 1902. Month and day defaulted, office addresses unconfirmed
stops.campa: He works as reader and editor for Rutten and Loening and begins Die Gesellschaft, a series that will run to forty volumes of social psychology, commissioning Simmel, Sombart, Landauer and Tonnies. Four years earlier he had helped found the Judischer Verlag with Berthold Feiwel, E. M. Lilien and Chaim Weizmann, a press for a national culture that had no nation to sit in. Editing is his trade for a decade, and it teaches him that a book is a form of address before it is a container.
stops.quote: Die Soziologie ist die Wissenschaft von den Formen des Zwischenmenschlichen.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, quoted in E. Wiehn (1991), p. 192, as cited in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; the Wiehn volume was not seen directly
suggested_refs: The forty volumes of Die Gesellschaft, Rutten and Loening, 1906-1912

stops.name: Berlin-Zehlendorf, the house on the Vopeliuspfad
stops.date_confidence: residence 1907-1916 attested; the marriage year is 1907, correcting an earlier 1901, and its location is unattested with Munich only inferred from Paula's origin. Coordinate is the Zehlendorf district centre
stops.campa: Solomon Buber dies in 1906. Paula converts and they marry in 1907. The family takes a house on the Vopeliuspfad in the Berlin suburb of Zehlendorf and stays nine years. Here Buber writes the Hasidic books, Die Geschichten des Rabbi Nachman in 1906 and Die Legende des Baalschem in 1908, then Ekstatische Konfessionen in 1909, an anthology of mystics from every tradition that helps invent comparative mysticism as a field. He is retelling Podolian village tales in the literary German of Vienna, and knows it.
suggested_refs: Die Legende des Baalschem (1908) and Ekstatische Konfessionen (1909), written at Zehlendorf

stops.name: Medzhybizh, the town of the Baal Shem
stops.date_confidence: thematic anchor, not an itinerary stop: no consulted biography records Buber travelling here. Dated to the year of Die Legende des Baalschem. Coordinate corrected from a pin some nine kilometres west of the town
stops.campa: The Podolian town where Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, taught and lies buried is the centre of gravity of everything Buber publishes in these years, and he never goes to it. He works from printed collections and from what he heard as a boy in Galicia. Gershom Scholem will accuse him of turning the Hasidim into German neo-romantics. Jorge Luis Borges, reading the same current through Meyrink and a Madrid tertulia a decade later, takes the tales in exactly the shape Buber gave them.
stops.quote: In the coming world they will not ask me, 'Why were you not Moses?' They will ask me, 'Why were you not Zusya?'
stops.quote_source: Rabbi Zusya of Hanipol, as retold in Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim: The Early Masters, trans. Olga Marx (1947); wording from WIST Quotations and English Wikiquote, which agree. The book itself is lending-restricted on the Internet Archive and was not opened, so the page is secondary
suggested_refs: The grave of the Baal Shem Tov in the old Jewish cemetery at Medzhybizh

stops.name: Prague, the addresses to Bar Kochba
stops.date_confidence: the three addresses fall between 1909 and 1911; month and day defaulted, and the lecture hall is not identified in consulted sources
stops.campa: Three times between 1909 and 1911 he speaks to the Bar Kochba student association in Prague on Judaism, and a generation of Czech Jews walks out of the hall changed. Max Brod is in the audience. Franz Kafka reads the addresses and argues with them in his diaries. Buber tells them that Judaism is not a confession to be professed but a substance to be realised, and that the realising is theirs to do. It is his first mass audience and the first time the philosophy sounds like a summons.
suggested_refs: Drei Reden uber das Judentum, delivered to the Bar Kochba association and published 1911
sources: Paul Mendes-Flohr, Martin Buber: A Life of Faith and Dissent

stops.name: Heidelberg, Weber's Sunday circle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the connection is asserted from the corpus rather than confirmed against a Weber-Buber correspondence edition, and is dated only to the years around 1908-1914
stops.campa: Max Weber's house above the Neckar gathers Troeltsch, Jellinek, Simmel and the young Jaspers on Sunday afternoons, and Buber comes into that circle as the editor commissioning Die Gesellschaft. The two men correspond over the series. Weber is building a science of social action out of ideal types, instruments held at a distance from what they measure. Buber is moving the other way, toward a relation no type can hold and no third party can observe. They agree on the object and not on the instrument.
suggested_refs: The Weber Sunday circle at Ziegelhauser Landstrasse 17, Heidelberg

segments.name: Der Jude and the Hessian Town

stops.name: Berlin, Der Jude and the refugee committee
stops.date_confidence: year attested for both the journal's founding and the relief committee; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In the middle of the war he founds Der Jude with Salman Schocken and edits it until 1924, the leading forum of German-speaking Jewish thought, printing Scholem, Rosenzweig, Landauer and the whole Prague generation. In the same city and the same year he helps set up a committee for the Jewish refugees driven west out of the Russian front zone. The journal argues for Jewish cultural autonomy in Central Europe while the war that made the argument urgent is still killing the men who read it.
suggested_refs: The runs of Der Jude, 1916-1924, edited by Buber

stops.name: Heppenheim an der Bergstrasse, the house
stops.date_confidence: residence 1916-1938 attested; month and day defaulted, and the street address is not confirmed in consulted sources
stops.campa: The family leaves Berlin for Heppenheim an der Bergstrasse, a small Hessian wine town under the Odenwald, and stays twenty-two years. This is the house where I and Thou is written and where the Bible translation is drafted. Buber commutes to Frankfurt for the rest of his German life and does the work itself in a garden. Long after the war the building becomes the seat of the International Council of Christians and Jews, which is a use its wartime owner could not have foreseen and would have recognised.
suggested_refs: The Buber house at Heppenheim, later the seat of the International Council of Christians and Jews

stops.name: Carlsbad, the Twelfth Zionist Congress
stops.date_confidence: the Twelfth Congress met at Carlsbad in September 1921; the day of Buber's resolution is not specified in consulted sources
stops.campa: After seventeen years outside the movement's committees he comes back onto a congress floor, at Carlsbad, and puts the Arab question on it. His resolution demands that Jewish settlement in Palestine proceed in agreement with the Arabs living there and never against them, and that the two peoples share the country as equals rather than divide it. It passes in a softened form. He will spend the next forty-four years watching the softening continue, and will not stop coming back to the floor.
suggested_refs: The Arab resolution of the Twelfth Zionist Congress, Carlsbad 1921

stops.name: Darmstadt, Keyserling's School of Wisdom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a 1922 visit is asserted from the corpus and was not confirmed independently in this pass. The School of Wisdom was active 1920-1933
stops.campa: Hermann Keyserling's School of Wisdom at Darmstadt, half an hour up the Bergstrasse from Heppenheim, puts Rabindranath Tagore, Carl Jung, Max Scheler, Hans Driesch, Leo Frobenius and Richard Wilhelm in the same rooms and asks them what a human being is for. Buber lectures there in the years he is drafting I and Thou. The circle believes the West needs the East. Buber is not convinced the compass is the right instrument, and tells them the meeting is the thing, not the direction it is made in.
stops.quote: I have no doctrine. I only point to something. I point to a reality.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, sourced there to Martin Buber Werkausgabe I, p. 1114
suggested_refs: The Schule der Weisheit at Darmstadt and its published Tagungen, 1920-1933

segments.name: Ich und Du and the Scripture

stops.name: Heppenheim, Ich und Du
stops.date_confidence: written 1922, published 1923; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The book is written in the Heppenheim house and published in 1923, a hundred and twenty pages that divide everything sayable into two grammars. I and It handles, uses, measures and files. I and Thou has no object at all, only a presence, and cannot be held, only entered and lost and entered again. Buber says the first draft came in an involuntary rush after years of failing at it. Ronald Gregor Smith puts it into English in 1937; Walter Kaufmann does it again in 1970 and calls Smith's Thou a mistake.
stops.quote: To man the world is twofold, in accordance with his twofold attitude.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, I and Thou, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark, 1937), opening line of Part One, confirmed against the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: Ich und Du (Leipzig: Insel, 1923), first edition

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Freies Judisches Lehrhaus
stops.date_confidence: the Stanford Encyclopedia has him professor at Frankfurt 1923-1933, Wikipedia dates the honorary professorship to 1930, and the conflict is not resolved. The Lehrhaus closed around 1930 and was reopened by Buber in 1933, so the teaching is not continuous
stops.campa: He teaches at the university and at the Freies Judisches Lehrhaus, the house of adult Jewish learning Franz Rosenzweig founded in 1920, where Gershom Scholem, Erich Fromm and Siegfried Kracauer also teach and the students are lawyers and shopkeepers rather than scholars. The Frankfurt he works in is the city of the Judengasse, where Samuel Oppenheimer's dynasty of court factors began two centuries earlier. The Lehrhaus closes around 1930. Buber will reopen it in 1933, into a darker use.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, I and Thou, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark, 1937), Part One, confirmed against the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: The programmes of the Freies Judisches Lehrhaus, Frankfurt, 1920-1930 and 1933-1938

stops.name: Frankfurt, Rosenzweig's rooms: the Verdeutschung begins
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, and Rosenzweig's home address is not confirmed in consulted sources
stops.campa: Rosenzweig can no longer move or speak. He works a special typewriter with one finger, and later indicates letters on a board while his wife reads them off aloud. In this condition the two men begin the Verdeutschung der Schrift, a German Bible that tries to carry the breath-units and the root-repetitions of the Hebrew across unbroken. They are translating the text beneath which Nabucodonosor's scribes ration-listed the exiled king of Judah, and they are treating it as speech rather than as document.
suggested_refs: Die Schrift, verdeutscht von Martin Buber gemeinsam mit Franz Rosenzweig, first volumes from 1926

stops.name: Jerusalem, Brit Shalom at Arthur Ruppin's house
stops.date_confidence: the 1925 founding at Ruppin's home is attested; the coordinate marks the organisation's seat and not a place Buber stands in that year, since he is living at Heppenheim and does not reach Jerusalem until 1938
stops.campa: At Arthur Ruppin's house in Jerusalem a small group founds Brit Shalom, Covenant of Peace, to argue for one state of two equal peoples. Buber joins it from Heppenheim and will not set foot in the city for another thirteen years. Judah Magnes, Gershom Scholem, Hugo Bergmann and Hans Kohn are in it with him. It never has more than a few hundred members and it never wins a vote, and Buber holds the position it stated in 1925 without amendment until the day he dies.
suggested_refs: The Brit Shalom circular Sheifoteinu and the group's binationalist memoranda, from 1925

stops.name: Frankfurt, the death of Rosenzweig
stops.date_confidence: December 1929 attested; the day is not given in consulted sources and is a placeholder
stops.campa: Rosenzweig dies in December 1929, at forty-three, with the translation standing at the book of Isaiah. Buber carries it alone for thirty-two more years and finishes it in Jerusalem in 1961, by which time the German Jewry it was made for is not there to read it. The Lehrhaus the two of them built closes the year after the death. Eight years of friendship leave a Bible and a school. What they also leave is a way of arguing about revelation that neither man could have reached by himself.
stops.quote: Through the graciousness of its comings and the solemn sadness of its goings it leads you away to the Thou in which the parallel lines of relations meet.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, I and Thou, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark, 1937), Part One, p. 33; the pool's citation to p. 26 is corrected by the printed page markers in the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: The Buber-Rosenzweig correspondence on the Verdeutschung, 1925-1929

stops.name: Frankfurt, the honorary professorship
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the honorary professorship to 1930, the Stanford Encyclopedia gives a professorship from 1923; both readings are carried and neither is resolved. Coordinate is the historic Bockenheim campus
stops.campa: The University of Frankfurt makes him honorary professor of Jewish religious philosophy and ethics, the first chair of its kind in Germany, in a country three years away from putting its holder out of the building. He lectures on the history of religion and on the Bible. Konigtum Gottes appears in 1932 and argues that the covenant of ancient Israel was a working political constitution and not a figure of speech. The professorship lasts three years, which is the length of the room he is given.
stops.quote: The primary words are not isolated words, but combined words.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, I and Thou, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark, 1937), Part One, confirmed against the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: Konigtum Gottes (1932), the first volume of the unfinished study of messianism

stops.name: Frankfurt, the resignation and the Mittelstelle
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested and the resignation follows Hitler's appointment of 30 January 1933; the month is not given in consulted sources and the day is defaulted
stops.campa: Hitler takes power in January and Buber resigns his chair before the state can remove him from it, unwilling to be dismissed out of a post he can vacate. He is fifty-five. Within months he reopens the Lehrhaus and founds the Mittelstelle fur judische Erwachsenenbildung, the central office for Jewish adult education, and the work of a lifetime turns into emergency schooling for a population being legislated out of its own country. Enrolment rises every year the Reich narrows the ground.
suggested_refs: The teaching programme of the Mittelstelle fur judische Erwachsenenbildung, 1933-1938

stops.name: Germany, forbidden to lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the whole country, since the ban applies to public speech everywhere in it
stops.campa: On the fourth of October 1933 the authorities forbid him to lecture in public. The prohibition is precise rather than total: he may speak to Jews inside Jewish institutions and nowhere else, so the audience is fenced instead of silenced. He travels the country doing exactly that, teaching Bible and Hasidic texts to congregations who have suddenly understood why the material matters. A philosophy built on the word between two people is being administered into a smaller room, and it keeps working in the room.
suggested_refs: The Reich prohibition of 4 October 1933 on Buber's public lecturing

stops.name: Germany, struck from the Reich Chamber of Literature
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, and the coordinate is the whole country
stops.campa: In 1935 the Reich Chamber of Literature strikes him from its rolls, and the right to publish goes with the membership. Schocken keeps printing him for Jewish readers under the exemption that lets Jewish presses serve Jews. He is fifty-seven, one of the most widely translated Jewish thinkers alive, and legally not a writer. Invitations arrive from the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, which had refused him twice on political grounds. He takes three more years to go, and teaches until the last of them.
suggested_refs: Schocken Verlag's Jewish-readership imprints, 1933-1938

stops.name: Jerusalem, the arrival
stops.date_confidence: March 1938 attested; the day and the port of entry are not specified in consulted sources
stops.campa: He arrives in March 1938, at sixty, one of the last of the German-Jewish intellectuals to get out before the doors close. Paula comes with him. The Hebrew University has offered a chair after refusing him twice, on the ground that his politics were inconvenient. Hebrew is his fourth or fifth language and he now has to lecture in it. The city he lives in from this month is the one he has been arguing about since Carlsbad, and it turns out to have streets, water rationing and neighbours.
suggested_refs: The Hebrew University's call to Buber, 1938

stops.name: Heppenheim, the house ransacked
stops.date_confidence: attested to the night of the pogrom; the family is already in Jerusalem
stops.campa: On the ninth of November the pogrom runs through Germany and the house on the Bergstrasse is broken open and wrecked. The family is eight months gone; the library is what is lost. Twenty-two years of work were done in those rooms, including the book which says that a person becomes a self only by being addressed. The walls survive the war. In time the building opens as the seat of the International Council of Christians and Jews, which is what a house is for after a night like this one.
suggested_refs: The Heppenheim house after Kristallnacht, 9 November 1938

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the chair of social philosophy
stops.date_confidence: the 1938-1951 tenure is attested; the month is inferred from his March arrival. The coordinate is the canonical Mount Scopus pin inherited byte-identical from the Einstein journey, and sits south of the campus buildings, whose corrected position is 31.7936 by 35.2447
stops.campa: The Hebrew University appoints him to social philosophy on Mount Scopus, the hill Albert Einstein toured America to endow and lectured on in 1923. There is no chair in Jewish thought available to him, so he teaches sociology and anthropology and turns both toward the between: what happens among people rather than what happens to them. He holds the post until 1951. Students report that he lectures in Hebrew with a Galician accent, never raises his voice, and answers questions for longer than he lectures.
stops.quote: The problem is discussed many times whether I am a philosopher or a theologian or something else.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, 'Replies to My Critics,' in Schilpp and Friedman eds., The Philosophy of Martin Buber (1967), p. 689, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
suggested_refs: The Hebrew University's Mount Scopus campus, cut off from Jewish Jerusalem in 1948

stops.name: Abu Tor, the mixed neighbourhood
stops.date_confidence: residence from 1938 to the 1947-48 fighting is attested; the month of the move and the house number are not confirmed in consulted sources
stops.campa: The first Jerusalem house stands in Abu Tor, on the ridge south of the Old City, a neighbourhood where Jewish and Arab families live along the same streets. He chooses it deliberately. The binational state he argues for in conference rooms is a domestic arrangement before it is a constitutional one, and he means to live inside his own proposal. In 1947 the fighting takes the ridge and the Bubers leave with what they can carry. The argument outlives the address by eighteen years.
suggested_refs: The Abu Tor ridge, a mixed quarter until the fighting of 1947-1948

stops.name: Jerusalem, the founding of Ihud
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: With Judah Magnes and others he founds Ihud, Union, to press for a binational Arab-Jewish state against the Biltmore Programme's demand for a Jewish commonwealth. It is 1942 and the news from Europe is arriving. Buber argues that a people saved by dispossessing another people has not been saved in the sense he means by the word, and is answered, by most of the Yishuv, that the sense he means is a luxury available only to the living. He keeps saying it for the next twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Ihud memoranda to the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, 1946

stops.name: Talbiya, the house after the flight
stops.date_confidence: the move follows the flight from Abu Tor in 1947 or 1948 and the year is not fixed more closely; the Hovevei Zion Street address is cited in secondary literature only
stops.campa: Driven off the Abu Tor ridge, the Bubers move to Talbiya, a quarter of stone villas built by Arab Christian families who have themselves just fled it. He is entirely aware of what he is living in and says so in print, which does not endear him to his neighbours. The house fills with visitors for seventeen years: theologians, psychotherapists, kibbutzniks, Americans with notebooks. Here he finishes the Bible translation, writes his Moses, and receives a world that has decided he is a sage.
suggested_refs: The Buber house in Talbiya, Jerusalem, 1948-1965

stops.name: Jerusalem, the state proclaimed
stops.date_confidence: May 1948 attested; the coordinate is the canonical Old City pin shared with several journeys in the corpus, and the Old City is closed to him from this year
stops.campa: The state is declared in May and Buber accepts it, which surprises everyone who had taken him for a doctrinaire. He votes, pays his taxes, keeps his chair, and moves into what he calls loyal opposition: for Arab return, for equal citizenship, against military rule in the Arab villages, and, fourteen years later, against the execution of Adolf Eichmann. The Old City is shut to him from this year onward. He can see the wall of it from the ridge he used to live on.
suggested_refs: Buber's public letters on Arab citizenship and military rule, 1948-1965

stops.name: Talbiya, Paths in Utopia
stops.date_confidence: three editions and three years: Hebrew Netivot be-utopia 1946 or 1947, English Paths in Utopia 1949, German Pfade in Utopia 1950. The pool's pairing of the English year with the German title is corrected here
stops.campa: Netivot be-utopia appears first in Hebrew, then in English as Paths in Utopia in 1949 and in German the year after: a defence of the communal socialists Proudhon, Kropotkin and Landauer against the centralising Marxist line, and an argument that the kibbutz is the one experiment in Europe's utopian tradition that did not fail. He calls it a signal non-failure and refuses to call it more. It is the most political book he writes and it reads throughout as a book about relation.
suggested_refs: Netivot be-utopia (1947), Paths in Utopia (1949), Pfade in Utopia (1950)

stops.name: New York, the first American tour
stops.date_confidence: the 1951 tour is well attested; the venue list is drawn from general secondary accounts rather than a confirmed itinerary and is a reconstruction. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At seventy-three he crosses the Atlantic for the first time and lectures across the United States, at Union Theological Seminary among other places, on Hasidism and on the philosophy of dialogue. Reinhold Niebuhr and Paul Tillich are in the audience, and Protestant theology takes I and Thou into its bloodstream for the next twenty years. The lectures become The Eclipse of God, published in English in 1952: God has not died, the book argues, but has been obscured, by us, standing in the light.
suggested_refs: The Eclipse of God (Harper, 1952), drawn from the 1951 American lectures
sources: Maurice Friedman, Martin Buber's Life and Work

stops.name: Hamburg, the Goethe Prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the ceremony venue within the university and the date are not specified in consulted sources
stops.campa: Hamburg gives him the Hanseatic Goethe Prize and he travels to Germany to take it, six years after the camps. In Israel the decision is attacked as a betrayal, and the attack does not entirely stop for the rest of his life. Buber's position is that a people cannot be addressed collectively as guilty or collectively as forgiven, only person by person, and that refusing to speak to Germans at all would be the one course his own philosophy forbids him. He goes, and he keeps the argument in public.
suggested_refs: The Hanseatic Goethe Prize of the city of Hamburg, awarded 1951

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Paulskirche
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In St Paul's Church, where the parliament of 1848 sat, he accepts the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade and gives the address on genuine dialogue. He tells the hall that he is speaking to the Germans who refused, and to the many who did not act and know it, and that with the men who ordered and carried out the murder of his people he has nothing whatever in common as a human being. The applause and the protest are both loud. He softens neither half of the sentence for either party.
suggested_refs: Buber's Paulskirche address, Das echte Gesprach und die Moglichkeiten des Friedens, 27 September 1953

stops.name: Ann Arbor, the dialogue with Carl Rogers
stops.date_confidence: April 1957 attested; the day follows the published transcript and the campus building is not identified in consulted sources
stops.campa: On a stage at the University of Michigan he sits down with Carl Rogers and they argue for two hours about whether a therapist and a patient can meet as equals. Rogers says yes, in the moment of the encounter. Buber says the relation is real and is not mutual, because one of them came for help and the other is paid to give it. It is five years after his public quarrel with Carl Jung over Answer to Job. The transcript is still put in front of psychology students who have read neither man.
stops.quote: Through the Thou a man becomes I. That which confronts him comes and disappears, relational events condense, then are scattered, and in the change consciousness of the unchanging partner, of the I, grows clear, and each time stronger.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, I and Thou, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (Edinburgh: T. and T. Clark, 1937), Part One, p. 28, confirmed against the Internet Archive scan
suggested_refs: The published transcript of the Buber-Rogers dialogue, University of Michigan, April 1957
sources: Widely documented transcript of the 1957 Buber-Rogers dialogue

stops.name: Venice, the death of Paula
stops.date_confidence: the year and the city are attested; no consulted source gives the month, so month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Paula dies in Venice in 1958, on the way home from Europe, after fifty-nine years. Buber is eighty. He writes an elegy for her and does not write poetry again. Georg Munk had published novels and stories under that name for half a century, and had read every page of his before it went anywhere else. He goes back to Jerusalem alone and lives seven more years in the Talbiya house, where visitors keep arriving and the correspondence keeps growing, and answers all of it.
suggested_refs: Buber's elegy for Paula, written 1958

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Erasmus Prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted. The Israel Prize (1958) and Bialik Prize (1961) are folded into this stop
stops.campa: The prizes come in a row at the end: the Israel Prize for the humanities in 1958, the Bialik Prize for Jewish thought in 1961, the Erasmus Prize at Amsterdam in 1963. The state whose founding policy he opposed honours him. The Europe that expelled him honours him. He is nominated repeatedly for the Nobel and never gets it. At eighty-five he travels to collect this one in person, the last long journey, from a city with its own reasons for thinking about what happened to the Jews of the continent.
stops.quote: Greatness by nature includes a power, but not a will to power.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Martin Buber, Between Man and Man, trans. Ronald Gregor Smith (1965); no copy was fetched and the wording and placement are unconfirmed
suggested_refs: The Erasmus Prize citation, Amsterdam 1963

segments.name: The Mount of Those Who Rest

stops.name: Talbiya, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He dies at home in Talbiya on the thirteenth of June 1965, eighty-seven years old, having outlived Rosenzweig by thirty-six years, Paula by seven, and the German-Jewish world that made him by a quarter of a century. The Bible translation was finished four years earlier. The last work on his desk is a reply to his critics. The house fills with people who each believe they stood in a particular relation to him, and each of them is right, which is the only outcome the philosophy would accept.
suggested_refs: The Talbiya house on the day of his death, 13 June 1965

stops.name: Har HaMenuchot, the burial
stops.date_confidence: burial the day after the death is attested by Hebrew Wikipedia, which also describes the procession with the President in attendance; the coordinate corrects an earlier pin some two kilometres southeast of the cemetery
stops.campa: He is buried the next day on the western hillside of Har HaMenuchot, the Mount of Those Who Rest, in a funeral the President of Israel walks in. Maimonides, at the rationalist end of the same tradition, was carried to Tiberias eight hundred years earlier. Buber closes the dialogical end of it on a slope above a city he disputed with to the last week of his life. The Jewish National Fund had planted a forest in his name near the kibbutz of HaZore'a the year before he died.
suggested_refs: The Buber grave at Har HaMenuchot
The Martin Buber forest near kibbutz HaZore'a, planted 1964

stops.name: Givat Ram, the archive at the National Library
stops.date_confidence: no consulted source dates the transfer of the papers; the year is a placeholder set after the death and should be corrected when the accession record is found
stops.campa: His manuscripts and correspondence go to the National Library of Israel on the Givat Ram campus, which is the natural archive for a man who held that the word lives between people rather than inside either of them. In 1968 the German councils for Christian-Jewish cooperation establish the Buber-Rosenzweig Medal and have given it every year since. Andy Warhol silkscreens his face in 1980. Israel Post prints him on a stamp in 1999, and streets carry his name in eleven Israeli cities.
suggested_refs: The Martin Buber Archive, National Library of Israel, Givat Ram
Andy Warhol, Ten Portraits of Jews of the Twentieth Century (1980)
